title: What is RG 146 and who still needs it?
seoTitle: ASIC RG 146: who still needs it
description: RG 146 sets ASIC minimum training standards for financial product advisers. Who it still covers after the professional standards reforms and what it requires.
shortAnswer: RG 146 is Regulatory Guide 146, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) guide that sets minimum training standards for people who give financial product advice to retail clients. Since 1 January 2019 it no longer applies to relevant providers, who meet the professional standards instead. RG 146 still covers people who give general advice, personal advice on basic banking, general insurance or consumer credit insurance, and advice on time-sharing schemes.
keyTakeaways: RG 146 (issued July 2012) sets knowledge and skill requirements at two levels: Tier 1, broadly equivalent to an AQF Diploma, and Tier 2, broadly equivalent to an AQF Certificate III.
Relevant providers (personal advice to retail clients on relevant financial products) have been covered by the professional standards since 1 January 2019, not RG 146.
RG 146 still applies to general advice, personal advice on basic banking products, general insurance and consumer credit insurance, and advice on time-sharing schemes.
Licensees must have continuing training policies, with an annual training plan and records for each adviser. ASIC has not set minimum hours.
ASIC stopped approving courses for its Training Register on 25 September 2012, so licensees must check themselves that courses meet the RG 146 standards.
appliesTo: AFS licensees and representatives who give general advice to retail clients
Representatives giving personal advice on basic banking products, general insurance or consumer credit insurance
Training and education providers whose courses are used to meet the standards

blocks.text: RG 146 requires advisers to meet set knowledge requirements, and in some cases skill requirements, before they give advice, and requires licensees to keep them trained afterwards. ASIC's [RG 146 page](https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/find-a-document/regulatory-guides/rg-146-licensing-training-of-financial-product-advisers) describes it as setting out "minimum training standards that apply to advisers and how advisers can meet these training standards".

Under RG 146.6 of the [published guide](https://download.asic.gov.au/media/1240766/rg146-published-26-september-2012.pdf), the standards must be met at either the Tier 1 or Tier 2 education level. Tier 1 is broadly equivalent to the Diploma level of the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) and Tier 2 to the Certificate III level (see [AQF levels and learning outcomes](/regulations/aqf-levels-and-learning-outcomes)). RG 146.7 says the requirements vary with whether the adviser gives general or personal advice, and with the products they advise on. Knowledge requirements (generic and specialist) are in Appendix A and skill requirements in Appendix B.

RG 146.4 applies the standards to all natural persons who give financial product advice to retail clients, subject to limited exemptions in Section B of the guide. ASIC notes that Sections D and E of the guide, on how advisers meet the standards and how courses and advisers are assessed, have been under review since 24 September 2012.

RG 146 still applies to advisers who are not relevant providers. ASIC's editor's note on the RG 146 page says the training standards "no longer apply to relevant providers" because the professional standards reforms have applied to them since 1 January 2019.
ASIC lists who RG 146 continues to cover:

items: people who provide personal advice on basic banking products, general insurance and/or consumer credit insurance
individuals who provide financial product advice about a time-sharing scheme

blocks.text: The dividing line is the definition of relevant financial products in section 910A of the [Corporations Act 2001](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A00818/latest/text): financial products other than basic banking products, general insurance products and consumer credit insurance. ASIC now reads RG 146's Tier 1 products as relevant financial products and Tier 2 products as those that are not. In practice, RG 146 matters most for contact centre staff, bank branch staff, insurance sales and claims teams, and general advice roles in super funds and product issuers. Advisers giving personal advice on relevant products follow the separate [education and CPD requirements for financial advisers](/regulations/financial-adviser-education-and-cpd-requirements).

sections.heading: How do advisers meet the RG 146 standards?

blocks.text: The guide says advisers generally meet the standards by completing courses listed on the ASIC Training Register, or, for experienced advisers, by individual assessment by an authorised assessor (RG 146.8). Courses on basic deposit products and related non-cash payment products can be assessed by the licensee instead (RG 146.9 and RG 146.11).

The register no longer operates as a live approval list. ASIC's [Training Register page](https://www.asic.gov.au/online-services/search-asic-registers/other-registers/asic-training-register) says ASIC "stopped approving training courses on 25 September 2012", that the register's content is valid up to 24 September 2012, and that people should contact the training provider about whether courses completed after that date meet the standards in RG 146. The practical consequence is that the licensee carries the judgement: it needs to be able to show that a course maps to the relevant generic and specialist knowledge areas and skill requirements at the right tier.

sections.heading: What continuing training does RG 146 expect?

blocks.text: Licensees must have policies and procedures that make sure their advisers undertake continuing training to maintain and update the knowledge and skills appropriate to their activities (RG 146.14). ASIC ties this to the general obligations in section 912A(1)(e) and (f) of the Corporations Act, which require licensees to maintain competence and to ensure representatives are adequately trained and competent (RG 146.121).

RG 146.122 says the policies should include a person responsible for continuing training, an annual training plan for each adviser, records of each adviser's training, and a decision on how much training each adviser needs each year. RG 146.125 sets out what an annual plan should address:

items: Assess the adviser's training needs against the standards, especially if their functions change.
Identify gaps or weaknesses from the preceding year and the areas of focus.
Set objectives: the desired changes in knowledge, skills or performance by the end of the year.
Decide the structure of the program, including training methods.
Assess whether the adviser met the objectives.
Give the adviser feedback on their performance.

blocks.text: ASIC has not prescribed minimum annual hours (RG 146.130). Licensees should nominate an appropriate figure based on each adviser's activities and experience. Group plans are acceptable if they still address each step and each person only performs the tasks their training equips them for (RG 146.128). The guide on [building a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) shows one way to record this by role.

sections.heading: What evidence should a licensee keep?

blocks.text: A licensee should be able to show, for each adviser, the standard that applies, how it was met, and what continuing training followed. RG 146.126 says keeping a record of each representative's training is a licence condition, and that licensees should keep written training plans updated at least annually plus evidence such as receipts, enrolment records, attendance lists and detailed diary notes.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents the RG 146 knowledge and skill areas as a framework, then maps each course and assessment to the areas it covers and the tier it meets. Because ASIC no longer approves courses, that mapping is the licensee's evidence, and it can be kept current as products and roles change.

faqs.a: RG 146 is a set of training standards in an ASIC regulatory guide, not a qualification in itself. People often say they are RG 146 compliant when they have completed a course mapped to the Tier 1 or Tier 2 knowledge and skill requirements for their advice activities.

faqs.q: Do financial planners still need RG 146?
faqs.a: No. Advisers who give personal advice to retail clients on relevant financial products are relevant providers, and since 1 January 2019 they must meet the professional standards: an approved qualification, the exam, the professional year where required, CPD and the Code of Ethics. ASIC says RG 146 no longer applies to them.

faqs.q: Does RG 146 set minimum CPD hours?
faqs.a: No. RG 146.130 says ASIC has not prescribed a minimum number of continuing training hours because the time needed varies with the adviser's activities and experience. Licensees should nominate an appropriate figure for each adviser and record it in the annual training plan.

faqs.q: Can a licensee assess a course itself?
faqs.a: For basic deposit products and related non-cash payment products, RG 146 allows the licensee to assess whether a course meets the relevant requirements. For other products the guide refers to courses on the ASIC Training Register or individual assessment by an authorised assessor, but the register stopped taking new courses in 2012.

factCheck.claim: RG 146 no longer applies to relevant providers; it continues to apply to general advice, personal advice on basic banking, general insurance and consumer credit insurance, and time-sharing schemes
Tier 1 is broadly equivalent to AQF Diploma and Tier 2 to AQF Certificate III (RG 146.6)
ASIC stopped approving training courses on 25 September 2012; register content valid to 24 September 2012
Licensees must implement continuing training policies (RG 146.14); annual training plan steps (RG 146.125); no prescribed minimum hours (RG 146.130); link to s912A(1)(e) and (f) (RG 146.121)

Advisers generally meet the standards via Training Register courses or individual assessment by an authorised assessor (RG 146.8); licensee assessed courses for basic deposit products (RG 146.9, RG 146.11); record keeping as a licence condition with evidence such as enrolment records and attendance lists (RG 146.126); group plans (RG 146.128)
Relevant financial products are financial products other than basic banking products, general insurance and consumer credit insurance (s910A), as summarised by ASIC
